case_studies.title: SLIM: Saturation-Aware Lightweight Performance Modeling for LLM Serving
case_studies.abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving commonly increases batch size to improve throughput, but performance eventually reaches a deployment-dependent plateau beyond which larger batches provide marginal gains while increasing latency and GPU memory consumption. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of optimizing large language model serving performance by identifying the causes of performance plateaus. The researchers built a performance modeling tool called SLIM to study the saturation points of GPU performance. The result is a better understanding of how to optimize batch size for improved throughput without increasing latency and memory consumption.

case_studies.title: PTP: Previous-Token Prediction based LLM Inversion for Near-Exact Prompt Reconstruction
case_studies.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generate text by auto-regressively sampling the next token. This inherently leads to a many-to-many mapping between prompts and responses, complicating the task of inferring prompts from observed outputs. Prior work on LLM inversion frames prompt recovery as a semantic reconstruction task. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of inferring prompts from observed outputs in large language models, building a system called PTP that can reconstruct near-exact prompts, and achieving a breakthrough in LLM inversion. The result is a functional approach to inverting language models in a black-box setting. This is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.

case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluating AI-text detectors by introducing a benchmark dataset that tests their performance on human-authored content rewritten by large language models. The authors built the Authorship-Rewriting Benchmark (ARB) dataset, which consists of 1,800 human source texts rewritten by four open-weight generators. case_studies.abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents based on large language models are increasingly deployed across mobile, web, and desktop environments. case_studies.title: Zero-Mem: Zero-Token Memory Operations for LLM Agents
case_studies.abstract: LLM agents need memory to act consistently over long interactions, yet many systems use additional LLM calls to operate that memory. Generating intermediate records and mediating their retrieval adds recurring token and time costs, while omitted or merged details can obscure the original evidence. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of inefficient memory operations for Large Language Model (LLM) agents by introducing zero-token memory operations, which eliminates the need for additional LLM calls. The researchers built Zero-Mem, a system that preserves original information without generating intermediate records. The result is a more efficient and cost-effective way to manage memory for LLM agents.

case_studies.title: Self-Play Meets Skill Evolution: Self-Evolving Search Agents that Pose, Solve, and Remember
case_studies.abstract: Self-play agents can generate training problems without questions from target benchmarks, but their curricula lack persistent state: failures affect gradients yet do not explicitly shape future practice. External skill memories preserve procedural experience but are typically learned from fixed task distributions. We introduce \textbf{SESA} (Self-Evolving Skill-Augmented Agent), which makes procedural memory an evolving state of tool-augmented search self-play. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of self-play agents lacking persistent state by introducing SESA, a self-evolving skill-augmented agent that poses, solves, and remembers problems. The result is an agent that can generate and learn from its own failures, improving its skills over time. This research is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.

case_studies.title: Fragility of Value under Imperfect Alignment
case_studies.abstract: As more responsibility is placed upon AI systems, it becomes increasingly important to guarantee that these systems are aligned with humanity. A common fear in AI safety is that human value is fragile -- that is, optimizing too heavily for an imperfect proxy to human values will lead to a catastrophic outcome. In this paper, we present a model of the alignment problem where an agent undergoes idealized alignment training that guarantees its value function satisfies a proxy condition before optimizing the world. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of AI systems not aligning with human values, by building a model that guarantees an agent's value function satisfies a proxy condition before optimizing the world, resulting in a better understanding of how to prevent catastrophic outcomes. The model identifies conditions on the human value function and the accuracy of the proxy, which can help prevent misalignment. The research focuses on AI safety and value alignment, which is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.

We introduce STAIR, a framework that converts historical repair trajectories into hierarchical, reusable plans that can be adapted to steer future repairs. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of LLM-driven repair agents treating every issue independently by building a framework called STAIR that converts historical repair trajectories into reusable plans. STAIR transforms past trajectories into multi-level trees that encode experience at several granularities, allowing for more efficient future repairs. The result is a framework that can adapt to steer future repairs, making the repair process more efficient.

case_studies.title: HAM-VLN: Harnessing Hierarchical Agentic Memory for Zero-Shot Vision-and-Language Navigation
case_studies.abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) enables robots to follow instructions in previously unseen environments. Recently, a training-free paradigm has emerged: the robot queries a multimodal LLM to understand its observations and plan the next action. However, long-horizon navigation based on either image streams or dense map inevitably introduces a growing memory and reasoning bottleneck. The result is a more efficient and effective navigation system. This research is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.

case_studies.title: TokTier: Exact Stateful Tokenization for Agentic LLM Serving
case_studies.abstract: LLM serving systems cache prompt KV state, yet most front ends still re-tokenize the full request text on every call. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of inefficient tokenization in large language model serving systems by building a system called TokTier, which achieves exact stateful tokenization. The result is a significant reduction in tokenization time, reaching up to 64% of the total time. This research improves the performance of language model serving systems.

case_studies.abstract: As LLMs evolve from code completion systems into autonomous scientific agents, evaluating their ability to conduct experiments has become increasingly important. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluating large language models (LLMs) as agents that can optimize hyperparameters in machine learning tasks. The result is a more comprehensive assessment of LLMs' capabilities in autonomous scientific tasks.
